Current required supplier statement (batch3, homesr-worldlines-and-clocks, computed level7): Let (A,V,eta,C^+) be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space (def-sr-affine-minkowski-model) and let I be an order-convex subset of R with at least two elements (def-interval); a curve of the model is a map x: I -> A. (a) Derivative and regularity of the parametrization. For s in I and h nonzero with s + h in I the difference quotient (x(s+h) - x(s))/h is an element of V, the displacement from x(s) to x(s+h) divided by the real number h; the curve is differentiable at s when the limit of these quotients as h -> 0 exists in the finite-dimensional real vector space V, and then this limit, written x'(s) in V, is the tangent vector of x at s. If x_A: A -> R^4 is the chart of an inertial frame (def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart), then x is differentiable at s exactly when the R^4-valued map x_A o x is differentiable at s in the sense of def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral, and then x'(s) = E((x_A o x)'(s)), where E: R^4 -> V is the frame isomorphism; this does not depend on the inertial chart used, because inertial chart transitions are affine, hence smooth (lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas), and all norms on the finite-dimensional V give the same limit. The curve is C^1 when it is differentiable at every point of I and the derivative map s |-> x'(s), I -> V, is continuous (def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity); it is C^k for k >= 1 when x' is C^{k-1}. A curve on a compact interval [a,b] contained in I is piecewise C^1 when there is a finite partition a = s_0 < s_1 < ... < s_m = b such that x is C^1 on every open subinterval (s_{i-1},s_i) and the finite one-sided difference-quotient derivatives at both ends of every piece exist in V. These are limits of (x(t+h)-x(t))/h over the relevant side of the piece, not assertions that x'(s) has a limit as s approaches a corner. Their finiteness implies continuity of x at the corners. No continuous extension of the open-piece derivative is required. Derivatives at the endpoints of I are the one-sided difference-quotient limits over I. (b) Causal character. Let x be differentiable at s in I. Then x is regular at s if x'(s) is not the zero vector; x is timelike (respectively null, spacelike, causal) at s if the vector x'(s) is timelike (respectively null, spacelike, causal) in the sense of def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors, and x is future-directed at s if x'(s) is future timelike or future null in the sense of def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets. The zero vector has no causal character, so only a regular curve has a causal character at s. (c) Worldlines. A future timelike worldline (massive worldline) is a C^1 curve x: I -> A with x'(s) future timelike for every s in I; a future causal curve (respectively a future null curve) is a C^1 curve with x'(s) future causal (respectively future null) for every s in I. A piecewise C^1 worldline is a piecewise C^1 curve whose tangents at every point of each open smooth piece and whose finite one-sided difference-quotient tangents at both endpoints of every piece are future timelike, and a C^k worldline is a worldline whose parametrization is C^k; C^2 regularity is what makes the four-acceleration of this page available. The parametrization is part of the curve: the image of a future timelike worldline is also the image of the past-directed curve s |-> x(-s), which is not a worldline of this model, and no worldline or clock claim is attached to it. The definition asserts the existence of no worldline beyond those given by an explicit formula. Current consumer use and hypotheses: Definition item. Obligations: (i) the division by $\tau'$ is legitimate because $\tau'>0$ ([[lem-sr-proper-time-parametrization]]); (ii) the equivalence $\dot P(s)=(P\circ\rho)'(\tau(s))$ is the chain rule along the reparametrisation, $\rho$ being the inverse of the increasing function $\tau$; (iii) componentwise differentiation in one affine basis and change of basis commute because the transition map is constant and linear, so the definition is basis-free; (iv) no dynamics is imported: $F$ is a derived vector field attached to a given $P$, not a prescribed law. No choice principle is used. $$\theta(\mathbf x,t):=\langle\mathbf k,\mathbf x\rangle-\omega t\in\mathbb R .$$

Let $\exp$ be the complex exponential of [[def-complex-exponential]] (the power series $\sum_{n\ge0}z^n/n!$, convergent for every $z\in\mathbb C$), let $\operatorname{Re}$ be the real part of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], and let $i$ be the imaginary unit of [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]].

For each $t\in\mathbb R$ define maps $\mathbf E(\cdot,t),\mathbf B(\cdot,t):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ componentwise by

$$E_j(\mathbf x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e_j\exp\bigl(i\,\theta(\mathbf x,t)\bigr)\bigr),\qquad B_j(\mathbf x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(b_j\exp\bigl(i\,\theta(\mathbf x,t)\bigr)\bigr),\qquad j\in\{1,2,3\}.$$

Equivalently, $\mathbf E(\cdot,t)$ is the real part, taken componentwise, of the complex vector $\mathbf e\exp(i\theta(\mathbf x,t))$, and likewise for $\mathbf B(\cdot,t)$ with $\mathbf b$ in place of $\mathbf e$.

### Well-definedness and conventions

For every $(\mathbf x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ the number $\theta(\mathbf x,t)$ is real, so $i\,\theta(\mathbf x,t)$ is a complex number and $\exp(i\,\theta(\mathbf x,t))$ is defined by the everywhere-convergent exponential series; multiplying by the complex number $e_j$ or $b_j$ and taking real parts is likewise defined. Both amplitudes may be zero, in which case the corresponding field vanishes identically. The joint map $(\mathbf x,t)\mapsto(\mathbf E(\mathbf x,t),\mathbf B(\mathbf x,t))$ has $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, an open subset of $\mathbb R^4$, as its domain, so the $C^k$ conventions of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]] apply to any regularity statement made about it; this definition asserts no regularity of its own beyond well-definedness. The symbols $\mathbf e$ and $\mathbf b$ are constant complex amplitudes, not fields; the complex quantity $\mathbf e\exp(i\theta(\mathbf x,t))$ is an auxiliary object whose real part is the field. Real parts, imaginary parts and complex conjugation are the explicit operations of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]. Since $\operatorname{Re}$ is additive and commutes with real scalar multiples, any identity obtained from the encoded expressions by sums, real scalar multiples, partial differentiation or integration may be projected by $\operatorname{Re}$ term by term; identities that multiply two encoded real fields may not be read off from a product of complex expressions without conjugation, and the correct second-order average rule is proved separately. Let J: Omega -> V, k, and T be a C^k vector field, a C^k covector field and a C^k type-(r,s) tensor field on Omega in the sense of def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space, with components J^a, k_a and T^{a_1...a_r}_{b_1...b_s} in the chart x, and primed components in the chart x'. Then: (i) J'^a = Lambda^a_b J^b: a contravariant index gains the factor Lambda^a_b, i.e. components transform by multiplication with the transition matrix. (ii) k'_a = (Lambda^{-1})^b_a k_b: a covariant index gains the factor (Lambda^{-1})^b_a. If theta(p) = k_a x^a(p) + theta_0 is an affine scalar function with constant covector k and constant theta_0, then theta(p) = k'_a x'^a(p) + theta'_0 with k' as above and theta'_0 := theta_0 - k'_a b^a, so the phase function is invariant when the constant term is transformed together with the covector. (iii) T'^{a_1...a_r}_{b_1...b_s} = Lambda^{a_1}_{c_1} ... Lambda^{a_r}_{c_r} (Lambda^{-1})^{d_1}_{b_1} ... (Lambda^{-1})^{d_s}_{b_s} T^{c_1...c_r}_{d_1...d_s}: every contravariant index gains a factor Lambda and every covariant index a factor Lambda^{-1}, and the law is consistent with the multilinear evaluation of T(p) after substituting the transformed basis. Every contraction of one contravariant with one covariant index is invariant, and the metric components satisfy eta'_{ab} = eta_{ab}. (iv) The coordinate partial derivatives satisfy partial'_a = (Lambda^{-1})^b_a partial_b wherever the derivatives exist. Consequently the divergence of a vector field is invariant, partial'_a J'^a = partial_a J^a, and for a C^1 type-(2,0) field T one has partial'_a T'^{ab} = Lambda^b_c partial_a T^{ac}. (v) Alternating covariant tensor fields transform by the covariant law on each slot; the oriented volume form of the model satisfies epsilon'_{abcd} = epsilon_{abcd}, since det Lambda = +1, whereas a general Lorentz matrix with det = -1 changes its sign. (vi) Let J be a C^1 vector field with components (J^0,J^1,J^2,J^3) in an inertial chart, and write the spatial block as J_cov := (J^1,J^2,J^3) and denote by partial_i the spatial partial derivatives in the chart. Then the continuity equation partial_a J^a = 0 is equivalent to partial_0 J^0 + sum_i partial_i J^i = 0, and under the passive boost with parameter beta (Lambda = B(beta), Lambda^{-1} = B(-beta)) the components transform as J'^0 = gamma(J^0 - beta . J_cov), J'_cov = J_cov + ((gamma - 1)/|beta|^2)(beta . J_cov) beta - gamma beta J^0. (vii) If U is a C^1 future timelike vector field and rho_0 a C^1 scalar field, then J:=rho_0 U is a C^1 vector field and its first component is J^0=rho_0 U^0. Future timelikeness gives U^0>0 in every inertial chart, so define the normalized chart direction u:=U/U^0 and the coordinate density rho:=J^0. Then u^0=1, u^i=U^i/U^0, rho=rho_0 U^0, and J=rho u pointwise. The coordinate density rho and scalar multiplier rho_0 are different objects: rho=rho_0 if and only if rho_0(U^0−1)=0; at points where rho_0!=0 equality holds exactly when U^0=1. The vector u is a normalized chart direction; it is not assumed to have unit or four-velocity normalization. In an x^0=ct convention the associated spatial coordinate velocity, if interpreted as such, has components c u^i; physical current/density identification requires its own model premise. Interpretation boundary: the identification of a physical charge-current with a vector field, and of rho with a measured charge density, is a model premise of the electromagnetic framework; this item is a statement about the transformation of components of specified fields and does not by itself assert that any physical current transforms as a vector. Current required supplier statement (batch3, homesr-worldlines-and-clocks, computed level7): Let (A,V,eta,C^+) be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space (def-sr-affine-minkowski-model) and let I be an order-convex subset of R with at least two elements (def-interval); a curve of the model is a map x: I -> A. (a) Derivative and regularity of the parametrization. For s in I and h nonzero with s + h in I the difference quotient (x(s+h) - x(s))/h is an element of V, the displacement from x(s) to x(s+h) divided by the real number h; the curve is differentiable at s when the limit of these quotients as h -> 0 exists in the finite-dimensional real vector space V, and then this limit, written x'(s) in V, is the tangent vector of x at s. If x_A: A -> R^4 is the chart of an inertial frame (def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart), then x is differentiable at s exactly when the R^4-valued map x_A o x is differentiable at s in the sense of def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral, and then x'(s) = E((x_A o x)'(s)), where E: R^4 -> V is the frame isomorphism; this does not depend on the inertial chart used, because inertial chart transitions are affine, hence smooth (lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas), and all norms on the finite-dimensional V give the same limit. The curve is C^1 when it is differentiable at every point of I and the derivative map s |-> x'(s), I -> V, is continuous (def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity); it is C^k for k >= 1 when x' is C^{k-1}. A curve on a compact interval [a,b] contained in I is piecewise C^1 when there is a finite partition a = s_0 < s_1 < ... < s_m = b such that x is C^1 on every open subinterval (s_{i-1},s_i) and the finite one-sided difference-quotient derivatives at both ends of every piece exist in V. These are limits of (x(t+h)-x(t))/h over the relevant side of the piece, not assertions that x'(s) has a limit as s approaches a corner. Their finiteness implies continuity of x at the corners. No continuous extension of the open-piece derivative is required. Derivatives at the endpoints of I are the one-sided difference-quotient limits over I. (b) Causal character. Let x be differentiable at s in I. Then x is regular at s if x'(s) is not the zero vector; x is timelike (respectively null, spacelike, causal) at s if the vector x'(s) is timelike (respectively null, spacelike, causal) in the sense of def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors, and x is future-directed at s if x'(s) is future timelike or future null in the sense of def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets. The zero vector has no causal character, so only a regular curve has a causal character at s. (c) Worldlines. A future timelike worldline (massive worldline) is a C^1 curve x: I -> A with x'(s) future timelike for every s in I; a future causal curve (respectively a future null curve) is a C^1 curve with x'(s) future causal (respectively future null) for every s in I. A piecewise C^1 worldline is a piecewise C^1 curve whose tangents at every point of each open smooth piece and whose finite one-sided difference-quotient tangents at both endpoints of every piece are future timelike, and a C^k worldline is a worldline whose parametrization is C^k; C^2 regularity is what makes the four-acceleration of this page available. The parametrization is part of the curve: the image of a future timelike worldline is also the image of the past-directed curve s |-> x(-s), which is not a worldline of this model, and no worldline or clock claim is attached to it. The definition asserts the existence of no worldline beyond those given by an explicit formula. Current consumer use and hypotheses: Proof strategy. (a) In an inertial chart theta is the affine function x |-> k_a x^a + theta_0; composing with gamma and differentiating is the chain rule (thm-chain-rule, def-derivative), and the derivative of the affine part is the constant covector k applied to gamma'. (b) Write the worldline in proper-time parametrization, x = x(tau); then theta o x has derivative k(x'(tau)) = k(U(tau)) by (a) applied to the reparametrized curve, with the chain rule and the positivity of dtau/ds (lem-sr-proper-time-parametrization). (c) U is nonzero future timelike and k^sharp is nonzero future null, so eta(k^sharp,U) < 0 by lem-sr-future-causal-pairing-negative; by the defining property of k^sharp, k(U) = eta(k^sharp,U) < 0. (d) For an inertial observer, thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition(a),(d) gives eta(U,U) = -c^2 and the unit vector n = U/c; linearity gives k(U) = c k(n), and positivity is (c). Current required supplier statement (batch3, homesr-worldlines-and-clocks, computed level7): Let (A,V,eta,C^+) be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space (def-sr-affine-minkowski-model) and let I be an order-convex subset of R with at least two elements (def-interval); a curve of the model is a map x: I -> A. (a) Derivative and regularity of the parametrization. For s in I and h nonzero with s + h in I the difference quotient (x(s+h) - x(s))/h is an element of V, the displacement from x(s) to x(s+h) divided by the real number h; the curve is differentiable at s when the limit of these quotients as h -> 0 exists in the finite-dimensional real vector space V, and then this limit, written x'(s) in V, is the tangent vector of x at s. If x_A: A -> R^4 is the chart of an inertial frame (def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart), then x is differentiable at s exactly when the R^4-valued map x_A o x is differentiable at s in the sense of def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral, and then x'(s) = E((x_A o x)'(s)), where E: R^4 -> V is the frame isomorphism; this does not depend on the inertial chart used, because inertial chart transitions are affine, hence smooth (lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas), and all norms on the finite-dimensional V give the same limit. The curve is C^1 when it is differentiable at every point of I and the derivative map s |-> x'(s), I -> V, is continuous (def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity); it is C^k for k >= 1 when x' is C^{k-1}. A curve on a compact interval [a,b] contained in I is piecewise C^1 when there is a finite partition a = s_0 < s_1 < ... < s_m = b such that x is C^1 on every open subinterval (s_{i-1},s_i) and the finite one-sided difference-quotient derivatives at both ends of every piece exist in V. These are limits of (x(t+h)-x(t))/h over the relevant side of the piece, not assertions that x'(s) has a limit as s approaches a corner. Their finiteness implies continuity of x at the corners. No continuous extension of the open-piece derivative is required. Derivatives at the endpoints of I are the one-sided difference-quotient limits over I. (b) Causal character. Let x be differentiable at s in I. Then x is regular at s if x'(s) is not the zero vector; x is timelike (respectively null, spacelike, causal) at s if the vector x'(s) is timelike (respectively null, spacelike, causal) in the sense of def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors, and x is future-directed at s if x'(s) is future timelike or future null in the sense of def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets. The zero vector has no causal character, so only a regular curve has a causal character at s. (c) Worldlines. A future timelike worldline (massive worldline) is a C^1 curve x: I -> A with x'(s) future timelike for every s in I; a future causal curve (respectively a future null curve) is a C^1 curve with x'(s) future causal (respectively future null) for every s in I. A piecewise C^1 worldline is a piecewise C^1 curve whose tangents at every point of each open smooth piece and whose finite one-sided difference-quotient tangents at both endpoints of every piece are future timelike, and a C^k worldline is a worldline whose parametrization is C^k; C^2 regularity is what makes the four-acceleration of this page available. The parametrization is part of the curve: the image of a future timelike worldline is also the image of the past-directed curve s |-> x(-s), which is not a worldline of this model, and no worldline or clock claim is attached to it. The definition asserts the existence of no worldline beyond those given by an explicit formula. Current consumer use and hypotheses: Postulate: an adopted physical premise, not a theorem. Obligations: (i) $P=mU$ uses the four-velocity of [[def-sr-four-velocity-and-acceleration]] with its normalisation $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ of [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]; (ii) the measurement identification names the mathematical quantities $E_n,q_n,T_n$ of [[def-sr-observed-energy-momentum-and-kinetic-energy]] and the SI units of [[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]] and explicitly disclaims observation; (iii) conservation is stated for an isolated collision only, as an equality of the side totals of [[def-sr-collision-datum-and-conservation]], with no existence or mechanism claim; (iv) the equation of motion form is adopted only for a stipulated force, and no force law is adopted. Empirical support for the assumptions is a nonlogical relation of the framework, not a proof; the idealisations of point particles, ideal clocks and flat spacetime are inherited and must travel to consumers. Focused reconciliation concerns the corrected regularity/endpoint/proper-time/AC-DC or point-field interface actually used; preceding source reading is preserved rather than newly claimed. Supplier quote: Adopt as a physical postulate of this framework the following four equations for
the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and the sources of [[def-em-sources]] on the
laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
$\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and the SI units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional
derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and let
$\rho,J$ be continuous. Then, with the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivative
$\partial_t$ at fixed position of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$

(b) [Weak branch] Let instead $E,B$ be locally integrable $\mathbb R^3$-valued
fields and $\rho,J$ locally integrable scalar and vector fields on
$I\times\Omega$, identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Let
$\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\partial_t$ act as
distributional derivatives, componentwise, and let $\psi$ range over
$C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).
Then the same four identities hold in the sense of [[def-distribution]]: the
pairings

$$\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$$

all vanish for every such $\psi$, all derivatives being distributional
derivatives ([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(c) [Scope] The postulate contains no magnetic charge: $\operatorname{div}B=0$
and no magnetic-source term appears in $\operatorname{curl}E$. Sources that
are not locally integrable functions (point or sheet sources) are covered by
neither branch and require their own definition. The equations are adopted
classical vacuum physics in the named inertial chart; they are not deduced from
charge conservation, from empirical agreement or from the special-relativity
postulates, and this item by itself asserts no covariance under changes of
inertial frame.. Current supplier content_sha256=f327adb707d6ce76a60511d5549c01996252a81f694017149b0b4f35ad5d91a9, consumer content_sha256=623389616c23d64d254461a9f16f987cc03f8a9f954ddab09f49c64d10930205. No physical empirical conclusion added.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open. Let $S\subset\Omega$ be a compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface ([[def-codimension-and-hypersurface]], [[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]): every $p\in S$ has an open neighbourhood $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ and a $C^2$ diffeomorphism $\varphi:U\to\varphi(U)$ onto an open subset of $\mathbb R^3$ with $\varphi(S\cap U)=\varphi(U)\cap(\mathbb R^2\times\{0\})$, in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. A **two-sided presentation** of $S$ consists of a continuous unit normal field $n:S\to\mathbb R^3$ together with sides: $n(x)$ is orthogonal to $S$ at $x$ in the sense that $\langle n(x),\gamma'(0)\rangle=0$ for every $C^1$ path $\gamma:(-1,1)\to S$ with $\gamma(0)=x$ and $\lVert n(x)\rVert_2=1$; and $\Omega_-,\Omega_+\subseteq\Omega$ are open sets with

$$\Omega\setminus S=\Omega_-\cup\Omega_+,\qquad \Omega_-\cap\Omega_+=\varnothing,$$

such that for every $x\in S$ there is $\varepsilon=\varepsilon(x)>0$ with $x+sn(x)\in\Omega_+$ for all $0<s<\varepsilon$ and $x+sn(x)\in\Omega_-$ for all $-\varepsilon<s<0$. The normal $n$ points from the side $\Omega_-$ to the side $\Omega_+$; the orientation convention for normals is that of [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]].

**The surface distribution $\delta_S$.** For $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]) define

$$\delta_S(\psi):=\int_S\psi\,dS,$$

where the right-hand side is the surface integral of the restriction of $\psi$ to $S$, taken in the sense of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]; complex-valued $\psi$ are integrated componentwise in real and imaginary parts. For a continuous **density** $a:S\to\mathbb R$ define

$$a\delta_S(\psi):=\int_S a\,\psi\,dS .$$

Both are complex-linear functionals on $\mathcal D(\Omega)$, and both are distributions: $\delta_S,a\delta_S\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ ([[def-distribution]]).

**Jumps across $S$.** Let $F:\Omega\setminus S\to\mathbb R^3$ be a field that is of class $C^1$ on $\Omega_-$ and on $\Omega_+$ separately and has one-sided continuous traces: there are continuous maps $F_+,F_-:S\to\mathbb R^3$ with

$$F_+(x)=\lim_{\substack{y\to x\\ y\in\Omega_+}}F(y),\qquad F_-(x)=\lim_{\substack{y\to x\\ y\in\Omega_-}}F(y)$$

for every $x\in S$, the limits taken in $\mathbb R^3$. The **jump of $F$ across $S$** is the continuous map

$$[F]:=F_+-F_-:S\to\mathbb R^3 .$$

No continuity of $F$ across $S$ is assumed or implied; $F$ need not even be defined on $S$, and the two traces may differ.

### Well-definedness and finite order

*The surface functionals are distributions.* Fix a compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ and $\psi\in\mathcal D_K=\{\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega):\operatorname{supp}\psi\subseteq K\}$ with the seminorm $p_0(\psi)=\sup_K|\psi|$ of [[def-fixed-support-test-function-frechet-space]]. Since $\psi$ vanishes outside $K$ and is continuous, $\sup_S|\psi|\le p_0(\psi)$; and $\int_S|a\psi|\,dS\le\lVert a\rVert_{\infty,S}\sup_S|\psi|\,S(S)$ with $\lVert a\rVert_{\infty,S}<\infty$ by compactness of $S$ and continuity of $a$. Hence

$$|\delta_S(\psi)|\le S(S)\,p_0(\psi),\qquad |a\delta_S(\psi)|\le \lVert a\rVert_{\infty,S}\,S(S)\,p_0(\psi),$$

a finite-order estimate of order $0$ with constants independent of $K$; by the local finite-order characterization ([[thm-local-finite-order-characterization-of-distributions]]) both functionals are distributions. This is the sense in which boundedness on the compact interface and finiteness of the surface measure give continuity of finite order. Linearity is immediate from linearity of the integral; the pairing is complex bilinear with no conjugation, as in [[def-distribution]].

*The field has locally integrable components.* The hypersurface $S$ is a Lebesgue-null set of $\mathbb R^3$: by the slice-chart property it is covered by finitely many compact pieces each of which is, in suitable $C^2$ coordinates, a graph over a compact subset of a coordinate plane, hence has content zero ([[thm-graph-of-continuous-function-on-a-compact-set-has-content-zero]]), and each piece has content zero in the ambient coordinates because it is the image under the $C^1$ chart inverse of a compact content-zero set ([[lem-c-one-images-of-content-zero-compact-sets-have-content-zero]]); a finite union of compact content-zero sets is compact and null ([[lem-null-sets-in-rn-closed-under-subsets-and-countable-unions]]), hence has content zero ([[lem-compact-null-iff-content-zero-in-rn]]), so $S$ has content zero in the sense of [[def-null-and-content-zero-in-rn]]. Away from $S$, continuity also gives a neighbourhood with a finite bound at every point. For a compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, these neighbourhoods cover $K$; take a finite subcover and the maximum of its finitely many bounds. $$\int_K\lVert F\rVert_2\le M_K\lambda_3(K)<\infty,$$

The sign convention is fixed by the normal: $n$ points from $\Omega_-$ to $\Omega_+$, so $[F]=F_+-F_-$ is measured in the direction of $n$. $r(p)=(r^1(p),r^2(p),r^3(p))\in\mathbb R^3$, the standard basis of
$\mathbb R^3$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) labels the three coordinate

the unit $\mathrm s^{-1}$ in the SI conventions of [[def-em-si-conventions]].
Fix complex amplitudes $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$, where $e$ carries the unit
$\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $b$ the unit T of the electric and magnetic
fields of [[def-em-fields]]. Let $k\cdot x$ denote the Euclidean inner product
of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and let $\exp$ and $\operatorname{Re}$ be
those of the encoding definition [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]], whose
convention that physical fields are the real parts of complex expressions is
used throughout. Define, for each $t\in\mathbb R$, maps
$E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ by

$$E(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e\,\exp(i(k\cdot x-\omega t))\bigr),\qquad B(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(b\,\exp(i(k\cdot x-\omega t))\bigr),$$

componentwise, and put $|k|:=\sqrt{\langle k,k\rangle}$,
$\hat k:=k/|k|$ and $T:=2\pi/\omega$. Terminology: $k$ is the **wavevector**,
$\hat k$ the **propagation direction**, $|k|$ the **wavenumber**, $\omega$ the
**angular frequency**, $T$ the **period**, $e,b$ the **complex amplitudes**,
and $\theta(x,t):=k\cdot x-\omega t$ the **phase**. Then:

(a) [Objects, domain and regularity] Both maps are of class $C^\infty$ on
$\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ in the sense of
[[def-em-complex-plane-wave]]; on the whole-space laboratory region
$\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] they are an
electric and a magnetic field of [[def-em-fields]] of every finite class
$C^k$, $k\ge1$, read in the frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$.

(b) [Phase and periodicity] At fixed $x$ the map $t\mapsto\theta(x,t)$ is
affine with derivative $-\omega<0$, so the phase decreases in time (the
$e^{-i\omega t}$ convention); $E$ and $B$ depend on $(x,t)$ only through
$\theta$ and are $T$-periodic in $t$.

(c) [Zero and nonzero waves] $(E,B)$ is the identically zero pair on
$\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ if and only if $e=b=0$; call the wave
**nonzero** otherwise. The electric field alone determines $e$ and the
magnetic field alone determines $b$, because
$\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\theta})=0$ for all real $\theta$ forces $w=0$

asserts no field equation, no dispersion relation, no transversality, no
energy claim and no polarization classification; those are the content of

units and the propagation constant $c$ are those of

claimed.

### Well-definedness and conventions

real number, so $i\theta(x,t)$ is a complex number and
$\exp(i\theta(x,t))$ is defined by the everywhere-convergent exponential
series of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]]; multiplying by the complex number
$e_j$ or $b_j$ and taking real parts is likewise defined, so each $E_j$ and

$T=2\pi/\omega>0$ and $|k|>0$, so $\hat k$ is defined. The joint map
$(x,t)\mapsto(E(x,t),B(x,t))$ has the open set $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$
as its domain, and the $C^\infty$ assertion in (a) is the one proved in
[[def-em-complex-plane-wave]] for the encoded expressions; the statement of
this definition uses that regularity and adds no further analytic property.
The equivalence in (c) is the elementary injectivity of
$w\mapsto\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\cdot})$ on $\mathbb C^3$: if
$\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\theta})=0$ for every real $\theta$, then taking
$\theta=0$ gives $\operatorname{Re}w=0$ and taking $\theta=\pi/2$ gives
$\operatorname{Re}(iw)=-\operatorname{Im}w=0$, so $w=0$, and the converse is
immediate. The complex notation is an encoding of real fields and of real
linear equations, not a complex physical field; the symbols $e$ and $b$ are
constant complex amplitudes, not fields. No electromagnetic equation, no
matter model and no physical interpretation is introduced by this
definition; in particular the complex amplitudes need not satisfy the

(a) [Charge parameter] The framework takes a real **charge parameter**
$q\in\mathbb R$, measured in coulombs, attached to a source; its sign is the
sign of the source and it is a parameter of the model. Charge quantisation is
not asserted.

(b) [Smooth source fields] A **smooth (volume) source field** on
$\Omega\times I$ is a pair $(\rho,J)$ of maps $\rho:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$,
$J:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is continuous on $\Omega\times I$ and of
class $C^1$ wherever a displayed equation differentiates it; $\rho$ is the
**frame charge density** (C m$^{-3}$) and $J$ the **frame current density**
(A m$^{-2}$). For each fixed $t\in I$ retain the compact Jordan branch: if
$V\subseteq\Omega$ is compact and Jordan measurable, define

$$Q_R(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)dy$$

by [[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]], with integrability supplied by
[[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]. For the
full measurable-volume branch assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]),
as required by the published Lebesgue-measure interface. If $V$ is any bounded
Lebesgue-measurable subset with compact closure $\overline V\subseteq\Omega$,
define

$$Q(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)d\lambda_3(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}F_t(y)\mathbf{1}_V(y)d\lambda_3(y),$$

where $F_t=\rho(\cdot,t)$ on $\Omega$ and $0$ elsewhere; the signed integral is
defined through its positive and negative parts
([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]],
[[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]). The
function $F_t$ is Borel, and hence Lebesgue measurable: for every open
$O\subseteq\mathbb R$ its preimage inside the open set $\Omega$ is relatively
open in $\Omega$, hence open in $\mathbb R^3$, and the closed complement of
$\Omega$ is added precisely when $0\in O$
([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]],
[[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]). This integral is absolutely
finite: $\rho(\cdot,t)$ is bounded on the compact $\overline V$ by
[[thm-extreme-value-metric]], $V$ has finite Lebesgue measure by
[[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]], and the
monotonicity and homogeneity of the nonnegative integral
([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]) bound
$\int|F_t|\mathbf{1}_Vd\lambda_3\le M_t\lambda_3(V)<\infty$, the indicator
integral being its simple-function value
([[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]); the
positive and negative parts are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]. On
the compact Jordan branch, under the same Countable Choice assumption,
$Q=Q_R$ by [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]].
The

defined independently: for each oriented surface patch in $\Omega$ the current
flux at time $t$ is the surface integral of $J(\cdot,t)$ in the induced
orientation, as defined in [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]].

different objects, defined by their own pairings when the framework uses them.

and hence the component transformation law of
[[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]] for $j$ between inertial charts.
This is a model premise, not a theorem about physical currents.

(d) [Frame density, scalar multiplier and the normalized material branch]
Suppose additionally that the identified $j$ is $C^1$ and $j=\rho_0U$, with a
$C^1$ future timelike vector field $U$ and a $C^1$ real scalar multiplier
$\rho_0$. Since $U^0>0$, define the normalized chart direction $u:=U/U^0$, so
$u^0=1$, $u^i=U^i/U^0$. Then $j=(\rho_0U^0)u$ and, because the electromagnetic
convention is $j^0=c\rho$,

$$\rho=\rho_0U^0/c,\qquad J^i=\rho_0U^i=c\rho\,u^i.$$

Pointwise equality $\rho=\rho_0$ holds if and only if $\rho_0(U^0-c)=0$,
including the zero-multiplier case. Where $\rho_0\ne0$, equality is equivalent
to $U^0=c$, which does not alone imply $U^i=0$ for an arbitrary future timelike
$U$. Thus a scalar multiplier is not automatically a Lorentz rest charge
density. The direction $u$ is chart normalized, with no unit or
proper-four-velocity normalization imposed in this general branch; if its
coordinate velocity interpretation is adopted, the spatial velocity is
$v^i:=cu^i$.

For the separate convective source model, explicitly assume that $U$ is the
material proper-time four-velocity, normalized by $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ as in
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. This is an additional model
condition, not a consequence of the factorization $j=\rho_0U$. In that branch,
$U=\gamma(c,v)$, $|v|<c$, $\gamma=(1-|v|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, and

$$\rho=\gamma\rho_0,\qquad J=\rho v.$$

Here $\rho_0$ is the rest charge density of this stipulated convective model:
in a comoving inertial frame $U=(c,0,0,0)$ and $j=(c\rho_0,0,0,0)$. The
equality $\rho=\rho_0$ then holds exactly where $\rho_0=0$ or $v=0$
(equivalently $\gamma=1$). Both signs of charge and the zero-density case are
retained.

(e) [Scope] This definition fixes the source objects of the smooth branch and
their transformation interface. It asserts no conservation law (that is proved
for stated source classes) and no regularity of singular sources..
